intro.text: Nineteen prophets, seers and singers who spoke in the courts of the kings, from David to Jehoiakim. Most are known from a few verses, and their pages are short.

Samuel and Kings tell of Gad, Nathan, Ahijah, Shemaiah, Jehu son of Hanani and Huldah; Jeremiah tells of Urijah. The rest are known from Chronicles, with the Psalm titles and Ezra–Nehemiah for the three singers.

Chronicles names several of them as writers of the records of the reigns: “the book of Nathan the prophet”, “the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite”, “the visions of Iddo the seer”, “the book of Jehu the son of Hanani”.
None of those writings is among the books of the Bible; what they were is shown as a question on the pages concerned.
David's three heads of song, Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun, are said to “prophesy with harps, with psalteries, and with cymbals”.

prophets.name: Gad
prophets.title: The prophet Gad, “David’s seer”
prophets.tagline: Counsel in the hold, three choices after the census, and an altar on a threshing floor.

claim.text: Gad told David, then in the hold, to leave it for the land of Judah. Years later, after David had numbered the people, Gad brought him three choices from the LORD, and on the day the plague was stayed he told him to raise an altar on the threshing floor of Araunah.

quote.text: Thus saith the LORD, I offer thee three things; choose thee one of them, that I may do it unto thee.

how.text: The word came to him as a message to carry: “the word of the LORD came unto the prophet Gad, David’s seer, saying, Go and say unto David”.
Chronicles tells the same scene as “the LORD spake unto Gad, David’s seer”, and says that for the altar “the angel of the LORD commanded Gad to say to David” where to build it.
Chronicles names a written record: the acts of David are “written in the book of Samuel the seer, and in the book of Nathan the prophet, and in the book of Gad the seer”.
It also names him as one of those whose commandment ordered the temple music: “for so was the commandment of the LORD by his prophets”.

claim.text: While David's parents stayed with the king of Moab and David was “in the hold”, Gad told him to leave it for Judah, and David went to the forest of Hareth.

quotes.text: Abide not in the hold; depart, and get thee into the land of Judah.

claim.text: After David's heart smote him for numbering the people, Gad set before him three judgments: famine, flight before his enemies for three months, or three days of pestilence. David chose to “fall now into the hand of the LORD; for his mercies are great”.

quotes.text: now advise, and see what answer I shall return to him that sent me.

message.theme: The altar on the threshing floor

claim.text: When the angel's hand was stayed by the threshing floor of Araunah, Gad came “that day” and told David to rear an altar there, and David went up “according to the saying of Gad”. Chronicles calls the owner Ornan.

quotes.text: Go up, rear an altar unto the LORD in the threshingfloor of Araunah the Jebusite.

quote.text: Abide not in the hold; depart, and get thee into the land of Judah.
Shall seven years of famine come unto thee in thy land? or wilt thou flee three months before thine enemies, while they pursue thee? or that there be three days’ pestilence in thy land?

claim.text: Chronicles gives the first choice as “three years’ famine”.

words.to: David, on the day the plague was stayed

quote.text: Go up, rear an altar unto the LORD in the threshingfloor of Araunah the Jebusite.

claim.text: Named with Gad in the record of David's acts and in the commandment for the temple music.
His book is named first in the same list of records of David's acts.
The owner of the threshing floor where Gad told David to build the altar; David bought it.

places.name: Mizpeh of Moab
places.note: Where David left his parents with the king of Moab while he was in the hold

places.name: Forest of Hareth
places.note: Where David went after Gad's word

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: The threshing floor of Araunah, by Jerusalem, where the altar was built

scripture.text: Scripture does not tell how Gad's life ended. After the census story he is named only as the writer of a book of David's acts and, in Hezekiah's day, as one whose commandment had ordered the temple music.

tradition.text: Among the antiquities of Hebron the Jewish Encyclopedia lists “the tombs of Gad, Nathan the prophet, Abner”.
tradition.who: A local tradition at Hebron, listed in the Jewish Encyclopedia
tradition.when: reported 1904; its earliest source has not been identified

questions.question: Seven years of famine (2 Samuel 24:13) or three (1 Chronicles 21:12)?

views.label: Three is the original number
views.holders: A. F. Kirkpatrick (1881); the Pulpit Commentary (1880–1897); Ellicott's commentary (c. 1878–1884)

argument.text: The Greek Septuagint also reads “three years” in 2 Samuel (Brenton's translation), and three fits the three months and three days. Kirkpatrick calls the reading of the Septuagint and Chronicles “unquestionably to be preferred”; the Pulpit Commentary says three is “probably right”.

views.label: Both are right: seven counts the famine already past
views.holders: Geneva notes (1599); Matthew Poole (1683–1685); John Gill (1748–1763)

argument.text: Three years of famine had already come for Saul's sin (2 Samuel 21:1); the year of the census made a fourth, and three more would make seven. Poole also mentions the view that a copyist wrote seven for three; Gill reports that Josephus, the Targum, the Syriac and the Arabic have seven.

questions.question: Who wrote the books of Samuel, and what was “the book of Gad the seer”?

views.label: Samuel, Gad and Nathan wrote the book of Samuel
views.holders: The Talmud (Baba Batra 14b–15a), as reported by the Jewish Encyclopedia (1905)

argument.text: Rabbinical tradition gives Samuel chapters 1–24 of 1 Samuel and, “on the strength of I Chron. xxix. 29”, credits Gad and Nathan with the rest. The same article adds that modern scholars reject this joint authorship.

views.label: Writings used by the Chronicler
views.holders: E. G. Hirsch and W. H. Bennett, Jewish Encyclopedia (1903)

argument.text: They list “The Words of Gad the Seer” among the Chronicler's sources for David, “unless these references are to that portion of the former work which dealt with these kings”.

notSaid: Scripture gives no father, tribe or home for Gad.
It does not say when or how he became “David’s seer”.
The “book of Gad the seer” (1 Chronicles 29:29) is not among the books of the Bible; whether any of it survives in Samuel is a question above.
2 Samuel 24:19 says David went up “according to the saying of Gad”; neither account says what became of Gad afterwards.

prophets.name: Nathan
prophets.title: Nathan the prophet, at the court of David and Solomon
prophets.tagline: The promise of David's house, “Thou art the man”, and Solomon's anointing.

claim.text: When David wished to build a house for the ark, Nathan first told him to do all that was in his heart; that night the word of the LORD came to him, and he brought David the promise of a house. After Uriah's death the LORD sent him to David with the parable of the ewe lamb.

quote.text: Thou art the man.

claim.text: When Adonijah made himself king, Nathan counselled Bath-sheba and went in to David after her. David ordered Zadok and Nathan to anoint Solomon at Gihon; 1 Kings 1:39 names Zadok as the one who poured the oil, and Jonathan's report says “Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet have anointed him”.

quote.text: And let Zadok the priest and Nathan the prophet anoint him there king over Israel

how.text: The word came at night: “it came to pass that night, that the word of the LORD came unto Nathan”; what he told David is called “all this vision”.
His first answer to David, “Go, do all that is in thine heart”, was given before the word came that night; the word that came said that David would not build the house.
He was sent: “the LORD sent Nathan unto David”, and he began with a story put to the king as a case to judge.
Chronicles names a written record, “the book of Nathan the prophet”, for the acts of David and of Solomon.
The title of Psalm 51 sets the psalm “when Nathan the prophet came unto him, after he had gone in to Bath-sheba”.

claim.text: David would not build the LORD a house; the LORD would make David a house. His son would build a house for the LORD's name, and the throne of his kingdom would be established for ever. Chronicles gives the same word with small differences: where Samuel has “thine house and thy kingdom shall be established for ever before thee”, Chronicles has “I will settle him in mine house and in my kingdom for ever”.

quotes.text: Also the LORD telleth thee that he will make thee an house.
He shall build an house for my name, and I will stablish the throne of his kingdom for ever.

message.theme: “I will be his father, and he shall be my son”

claim.text: Nathan's word says of David's son: “I will be his father, and he shall be my son. If he commit iniquity, I will chasten him”. Chronicles' telling has “I will be his father, and he shall be my son” without the words about chastening. In Chronicles David also repeats the promise of Solomon by name, and Hebrews 1:5 quotes “I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son” of the Son.

The parable led David to condemn the rich man; Nathan then named David's own deed, the taking of Uriah's wife and his death “with the sword of the children of Ammon”, and said the sword would never depart from his house.

quotes.text: Now therefore the sword shall never depart from thine house

message.theme: Forgiven, yet the child would die

claim.text: When David said “I have sinned against the LORD”, Nathan answered that the LORD had put away his sin and he would not die, but the child born to him would die.

quotes.text: The LORD also hath put away thy sin; thou shalt not die.

message.theme: Who will sit on the throne

claim.text: In David's old age Nathan put Adonijah's feast before Bath-sheba and the king, and asked David whether he had said Adonijah should reign after him.

quotes.text: Is this thing done by my lord the king, and thou hast not shewed it unto thy servant, who should sit on the throne of my lord the king after him?

quote.text: Go, do all that is in thine heart; for the LORD is with thee.
Thou art the man.
Now therefore come, let me, I pray thee, give thee counsel, that thou mayest save thine own life, and the life of thy son Solomon.
My lord, O king, hast thou said, Adonijah shall reign after me, and he shall sit upon my throne?

claim.text: A parable told as a case for judgment: a rich man with many flocks took a poor man's one ewe lamb to feed a traveller.

word.text: Nathan's word: David's son “shall build an house for my name” (2 Samuel 7:13).

reported.text: At the temple's dedication Solomon says that the LORD “hath performed his word that he spake”, and that he has “built an house for the name of the LORD God of Israel”. He recalls the promise as made to David; he does not name Nathan.

claim.text: With Nathan and Benaiah he was not with Adonijah, and David sent the three to make Solomon king.
Named with Nathan among those Adonijah did not invite, and sent with him to Gihon.
Nathan counselled her to go in to David, and promised to come in after her and “confirm thy words”.
He called the king's sons to his feast but not Nathan; Nathan reported it to David.
Named with Nathan in the records of David's acts and in the commandment for the temple music.

person.name: Azariah and Zabud, “the son of Nathan”

claim.text: 1 Kings 4:5 names Azariah son of Nathan over Solomon's officers and Zabud son of Nathan as “principal officer, and the king’s friend”. Which Nathan is meant is a question below.

places.name: Gihon
places.note: Where Solomon was anointed

scripture.text: Scripture does not tell of Nathan's death. His last scene is Solomon's anointing; afterwards he is named only as the writer of a book and in Hezekiah's day.

tradition.text: “A grave at Halhul, near Hebron, is pointed out as that of Nathan, but this is doubtful.”
tradition.who: E. G. Hirsch and E. N. Calisch, Jewish Encyclopedia
tradition.when: 1905; the earliest source has not been identified

tradition.text: Hebron's antiquities are said to include “the tombs of Gad, Nathan the prophet, Abner”.
tradition.who: A local tradition at Hebron, listed in the Jewish Encyclopedia

questions.question: Who sent Nathan in 2 Samuel 12:25, and who named the child Jedidiah?

views.label: The LORD sent Nathan, who gave the name
views.holders: A. F. Kirkpatrick (1881); the Pulpit Commentary (1880–1897)

argument.text: Kirkpatrick: “Jehovah commissioned Nathan … to give the boy a second name, which he did accordingly.” The Pulpit Commentary: “the sense plainly is that God sent a message by Nathan.”

views.label: David put the child in Nathan's hand
views.holders: “Some commentators”, following the Latin Vulgate, as reported by Kirkpatrick and the Pulpit Commentary

argument.text: They read “he (David) committed him to the hand of Nathan” for his education. Kirkpatrick calls this explanation “doubtful”, with “no further trace of the fact”.

questions.question: Of whom is “he shall be my son” spoken?

views.label: Solomon and the kings of David's line
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1866)

argument.text: Keil: the promise “related primarily to Solomon, and had a certain fulfilment in him and his reign”. Chronicles has David apply it to Solomon by name.

views.label: Solomon first, and Christ in its fullest sense
views.holders: A. F. Kirkpatrick (1881); Ellicott's commentary (c. 1878–1884); John Gill (1748–1763)

argument.text: Kirkpatrick: it “finds its highest fulfilment” in the relation of the Father and the Son, for which Hebrews 1:5 quotes it. Ellicott: the promise of a throne for ever “can only be fulfilled … in the Messiah”.

questions.question: Were Azariah and Zabud, “the son of Nathan” (1 Kings 4:5), sons of the prophet?

views.label: Yes, the prophet's sons
views.holders: Matthew Poole (1683–1685); John Gill (1748–1763); Jewish Encyclopedia (1905); the site's person data

argument.text: Poole and Gill take them to be the prophet's sons, promoted by Solomon; the Jewish Encyclopedia says “Two sons of Nathan, Azariah and Zabud, are mentioned”.

views.label: No, sons of Nathan the son of David
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1872); Ellicott's commentary (c. 1878–1884)

argument.text: Keil: “Nathan is not the prophet of that name, … but the son of David mentioned in 2 Samuel 5:14”. Ellicott says “probably” David's son, since the prophet's title is given wherever he is first named in Kings.

views.label: It cannot be decided
views.holders: The Pulpit Commentary (1880–1897)

argument.text: “It is quite impossible to decide with certainty which is meant, if either.”

questions.question: What was the written record Chronicles names for David and Solomon (“the book of Nathan the prophet”)?

views.label: Writings used by the Chronicler, perhaps parts of a larger history
views.holders: E. G. Hirsch and W. H. Bennett, Jewish Encyclopedia (1903)

argument.text: They list the prophets' “words”, “visions” and “prophecy” among the Chronicler's sources, and take most of them to be sections of “The Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah”, “probably because the Prophets were supposed to have been the annalists”; for David and Solomon they allow that the references may be to “that portion of the former work which dealt with these kings”. 2 Chronicles 20:34 says the book of Jehu “is mentioned in the book of the kings of Israel”.

views.label: Histories written by the prophets themselves, now lost
views.holders: Matthew Poole (1683–1685); John Gill (1748–1763)

argument.text: Poole takes Iddo's book “concerning genealogies” as “an historical account written by him”; Gill says Iddo “might write the history of his own times”. None of these writings is among the books of the Bible.

notSaid: Scripture gives no father, tribe or home for Nathan, and does not tell how he became a prophet.
2 Samuel 12:25 does not say plainly who sent Nathan or who gave the name Jedidiah (see the question above).
Chronicles tells Nathan's promise to David (1 Chronicles 17) but not the parable or his part in Solomon's anointing.
Scripture does not itself say that Absalom's deed (2 Samuel 16:22) fulfilled Nathan's word about David's wives (2 Samuel 12:11).
This Nathan is a different man from Nathan the son of David (2 Samuel 5:14; Luke 3:31).

prophets.name: Heman
prophets.title: Heman the singer, “the king’s seer in the words of God” (1 Chronicles 25:5)
prophets.tagline: One of David's three heads of song, whose sons “prophesied” with instruments.

claim.text: When the ark was brought up, the Levites appointed Heman, with Asaph and Ethan, “to sound with cymbals of brass”. David and the captains of the host set apart the sons of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun to “prophesy with harps, with psalteries, and with cymbals”.

quote.text: All these were the sons of Heman the king’s seer in the words of God, to lift up the horn.

claim.text: At the dedication of the temple the singers “of Asaph, of Heman, of Jeduthun” stood at the east end of the altar.

how.text: Chronicles calls the singers' work prophecy: they “should prophesy with harps, with psalteries, and with cymbals”.
Heman is called “the king’s seer in the words of God, to lift up the horn”.
With Jeduthun he served before the tabernacle at Gibeon “with trumpets and cymbals for those that should make a sound, and with musical instruments of God”.

claim.text: Heman and Jeduthun were set at Gibeon “to give thanks to the LORD, because his mercy endureth for ever”.

signs.label: The cloud at the temple's dedication

claim.text: When the Levite singers “of Asaph, of Heman, of Jeduthun” and the trumpeters “were as one” in praise, “the house was filled with a cloud”.
“His brother Asaph” stood at his right hand.
Served with him at Gibeon; Chronicles names the third head of song Ethan in some places and Jeduthun in others.

1 Chronicles 6:33 calls Heman “the son of Joel, the son of Shemuel”, and the line goes on through Elkanah, Jeroham and Zuph as in 1 Samuel 1:1; Samuel's firstborn was Joel. Commentators take Heman to be Samuel's grandson (Ellicott; W. E. Barnes, who writes that Shemuel is “the well-known prophet”).
“God gave to Heman fourteen sons and three daughters”; his sons served “for song in the house of the LORD”.

places.name: Gibeon
places.note: Before the tabernacle in the high place

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: The temple's dedication

scripture.text: Scripture does not tell of Heman's death. His family went on: sons of Heman served under Hezekiah, and Josiah's singers kept the order of David, Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun.

questions.question: Is “Heman the Ezrahite” of Psalm 88 this Heman?

views.label: Yes, the singer
views.holders: R. Jamieson, A. R. Fausset and D. Brown (1871)

argument.text: They take Heman and Ethan of Psalms 88 and 89 to be David's singers, “probably adopted into the tribe of Judah” if they are also the wise men of 1 Kings 4:31.

views.label: Perhaps the wise man, son of Zerah
views.holders: E. G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn, Jewish Encyclopedia (1904), giving both sides

argument.text: The psalm's “for the sons of Korah” and the psalms of Asaph and Jeduthun point to the singer; but “Ezrahite” and the next psalm's “Ethan the Ezrahite” point to the sons of Zerah renowned for wisdom (1 Kings 4:31; 1 Chronicles 2:6), in which case the title “would be composed of two contradictory parts”.

notSaid: No words of Heman are quoted in Scripture, and Chronicles does not say what the singers' “prophesying” with instruments sounded like.
Scripture does not say that Heman wrote Psalm 88; its title names “Heman the Ezrahite” (see the question above).
1 Kings 4:31 names a Heman among the wise men Solomon surpassed; whether he is this Heman is not said.

prophets.name: Asaph
prophets.title: Asaph the singer, called “the seer” (2 Chronicles 29:30)
prophets.tagline: Chief of the singers before the ark; twelve psalms bear his name.

claim.text: David appointed Levites before the ark, “Asaph the chief”, and on that day “delivered first this psalm to thank the LORD into the hand of Asaph and his brethren”. Asaph's sons “prophesied according to the order of the king”.

quote.text: Then on that day David delivered first this psalm to thank the LORD into the hand of Asaph and his brethren.

claim.text: At the temple's dedication the singers “of Asaph, of Heman, of Jeduthun” stood at the east end of the altar.

how.text: He led with cymbals: “Asaph made a sound with cymbals”.
His sons were “under the hands of Asaph, which prophesied according to the order of the king”.
Chronicles calls him “Asaph the seer”, and Hezekiah's Levites sang “the words of David, and of Asaph”.
Twelve psalms carry his name in their titles: Psalm 50 and Psalms 73 to 83 (for example “A Psalm of Asaph”). The titles do not say when the psalms were written.

claim.text: David delivered a psalm of thanks into the hand of Asaph and his brethren; it begins “Give thanks unto the LORD, call upon his name”.

quotes.text: Give thanks unto the LORD, call upon his name, make known his deeds among the people.

claim.text: The returned singers were “the children of Asaph”, who praised at the laying of the temple's foundation “after the ordinance of David”; Nehemiah recalls that “in the days of David and Asaph of old there were chief of the singers”.

quotes.text: For in the days of David and Asaph of old there were chief of the singers, and songs of praise and thanksgiving unto God.

signs.label: The cloud at the temple's dedication

claim.text: When the Levite singers “of Asaph, of Heman, of Jeduthun” and the trumpeters “were as one” in praise, “the house was filled with a cloud”.
Asaph stood at Heman's right hand.
The third head of song, named with Asaph and Heman.
Asaph was “the son of Berachiah”, of the line of Gershom son of Levi.

person.name: Zaccur, Joseph, Nethaniah and Asarelah, his sons

claim.text: “The sons of Asaph under the hands of Asaph”.
A Levite of Asaph's line who prophesied before Jehoshaphat.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Before the ark in the tent David pitched for it

scripture.text: Scripture does not tell of Asaph's death. His line went on: Jahaziel, “a Levite of the sons of Asaph”, prophesied before Jehoshaphat; Hezekiah's Levites sang “the words of David, and of Asaph the seer”; at Josiah's passover “the singers the sons of Asaph were in their place”; and “the children of Asaph” are named among the singers who came back from the exile.

questions.question: Who wrote the psalms titled “of Asaph”?

views.label: Asaph, David's singer
views.holders: The titles as they stand; the Pulpit Commentary (1880–1897) on Psalm 73

argument.text: Hezekiah's Levites sang “the words of David, and of Asaph the seer”. The Pulpit Commentary notes that “the triumph of Absalom” has been suggested as the occasion of Psalm 73.

views.label: Later singers of Asaph's line or guild, for some of them
views.holders: R. Jamieson, A. R. Fausset and D. Brown (1871); A. F. Kirkpatrick (1895); M. Jastrow Jr. and others, Jewish Encyclopedia (1902)

argument.text: Psalm 74 laments a sanctuary burned and cast down. If that is the Babylonian conquest, JFB says the author was “probably a descendant and namesake” of Asaph; Kirkpatrick weighs Shishak's raid, the Babylonian conquest and the Maccabean age, and says that apart from the title “all other considerations are against” Shishak. The Jewish Encyclopedia calls Asaph the “Eponym of a musical gild”.

notSaid: 1 Chronicles 16:7 says David delivered the psalm into Asaph's hand; it does not say Asaph wrote it.
Scripture does not say when the psalms of Asaph were written.
Other men named Asaph are different people: the father of Joah the recorder (2 Kings 18:18) and the keeper of the king's forest (Nehemiah 2:8).

prophets.name: Jeduthun
otherNames: Ethan, if the two are one man (see the questions)
prophets.title: Jeduthun, “the king’s seer” (2 Chronicles 35:15)
prophets.tagline: A head of David's singers who “prophesied with a harp, to give thanks and to praise the LORD”.

claim.text: David and the captains of the host set apart the sons of Asaph, Heman and Jeduthun to prophesy with instruments; Jeduthun and Heman were left at Gibeon before the tabernacle.

quote.text: under the hands of their father Jeduthun, who prophesied with a harp, to give thanks and to praise the LORD.

claim.text: At the temple's dedication the singers “of Asaph, of Heman, of Jeduthun” stood at the east end of the altar.

how.text: He “prophesied with a harp, to give thanks and to praise the LORD”.
Chronicles calls him “Jeduthun the king’s seer”.
The titles of Psalms 39, 62 and 77 read “To the chief Musician, to Jeduthun” or “even to Jeduthun”.

claim.text: At Gibeon, with Heman, he was “to give thanks to the LORD, because his mercy endureth for ever”.

signs.label: The cloud at the temple's dedication

claim.text: When the Levite singers “of Asaph, of Heman, of Jeduthun” and the trumpeters “were as one” in praise, “the house was filled with a cloud”.
With him at Gibeon with trumpets and cymbals.
Named with him as heads of song.

person.name: Gedaliah, Zeri, Jeshaiah, Hashabiah and Mattithiah, his sons

claim.text: “Under the hands of their father Jeduthun”.
A porter before the ark.

places.name: Gibeon
places.note: Before the tabernacle in the high place

scripture.text: Scripture does not tell of his death. Sons of Jeduthun were among the Levites who cleansed the house of the LORD under Hezekiah, Josiah's singers kept the order of “David, and Asaph, and Heman, and Jeduthun the king’s seer”, and a descendant of Jeduthun served in Jerusalem after the exile.

questions.question: Is Jeduthun the same man as Ethan?

views.label: Yes, two names for one man
views.holders: John Gill (1748–1763); Ellicott's commentary (c. 1878–1884); E. G. Hirsch and E. König, Jewish Encyclopedia (1903)

argument.text: Ethan stands beside Heman and Asaph in 1 Chronicles 6 and 15, and Jeduthun in the same place in 1 Chronicles 16 and 25; Gill writes “Jeduthun; or Ethan”, and the Jewish Encyclopedia speaks of “Ethan-Jeduthun”. The site's person data also treats them as one.

views.label: Two families' traditions
views.holders: W. E. Barnes (1899)

argument.text: “Probably there was a variation in the tradition as to the third name, two families competing each for the honour of its own ancestor.”

questions.question: What does “to Jeduthun” mean in the titles of Psalms 39, 62 and 77?

views.label: The singer himself
views.holders: Geneva notes (1599); R. Jamieson, A. R. Fausset and D. Brown (1871)

argument.text: The Geneva note on Psalm 39: “This was one of the chief singers”. JFB: his name is mentioned “perhaps, as a special honor”.

views.label: Perhaps a musical direction
views.holders: E. G. Hirsch and I. M. Price, Jewish Encyclopedia (1904)

argument.text: The word in the titles may be “indicating some kind of musical direction or instrument”.

notSaid: 1 Chronicles 25:3 says Jeduthun had “six” sons but the King James text names five.
No words of Jeduthun are quoted, and Scripture does not say he wrote any psalm.
Whether Obed-edom “the son of Jeduthun” (1 Chronicles 16:38) is the Obed-edom the Gittite who kept the ark (2 Samuel 6:10) is not said.

prophets.name: Iddo
prophets.title: Iddo the seer, known only as a writer
prophets.tagline: Named three times in Chronicles, always as the author of a record.

claim.text: The acts of Solomon are written, among other places, in “the visions of Iddo the seer against Jeroboam the son of Nebat”.
Iddo's visions were “against Jeroboam the son of Nebat”; their words are not given.
Rehoboam's acts are written “in the book of Shemaiah the prophet, and of Iddo the seer concerning genealogies”.
Abijah's acts, ways and sayings “are written in the story of the prophet Iddo”.

how.text: Chronicles calls him “the seer” twice and “the prophet” once, and names three records: “visions”, a book “concerning genealogies”, and a “story”.
The word rendered “story” is the Hebrew midrash; W. E. Barnes notes that the Revised Version renders it “commentary”.

claim.text: Their records are named together for Rehoboam's reign.
Named with Iddo as the writers of Solomon's acts.

scripture.text: Scripture says nothing of Iddo's life or death.

tradition.text: Josephus calls the man of God who cried against Jeroboam's altar (1 Kings 13) “a prophet, whose name was Jadon”. The Jewish Encyclopedia takes this, and Jerome, as identifying him with Iddo; if so, Iddo is the man of God killed by a lion on his way home.
tradition.who: Josephus, Antiquities 8.8.5; Jerome, Hebrew Questions on Chronicles

questions.question: Is Iddo the unnamed “man of God out of Judah” of 1 Kings 13?

views.label: Yes
views.holders: Josephus (about AD 93) and Jerome (about AD 400), as read by the Jewish Encyclopedia (1904)

argument.text: Because Iddo's visions were “against Jeroboam”, he “has been identified” with the prophet who denounced Jeroboam's altar.

views.label: Scripture's account
views.holders: The text of 1 Kings 13

argument.text: Kings never names the man of God; it calls him only “a man of God out of Judah”.

questions.question: Is Iddo the Oded of 2 Chronicles 15:8?

views.label: Yes
views.holders: Jerome, as reported by the Jewish Encyclopedia (1904)

argument.text: “Jerome identifies Iddo also with the Oded of II Chron. xv. 8.”

views.label: No
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1872)

argument.text: Keil: the conjecture “that עודד was the same person as עדּו” has “no tenable foundation”.

questions.question: Were the books of Shemaiah and Iddo one work?

views.label: Probably one book
views.holders: W. E. Barnes (1899)

argument.text: “Probably one book is meant, begun by Shemaiah and continued by Iddo”; “concerning genealogies” may be the book's title.

views.label: Sections of a larger history
views.holders: E. G. Hirsch and W. H. Bennett, Jewish Encyclopedia (1903)

argument.text: They list “The Words of Shemaiah the Prophet and of Iddo the Seer” among sections of “The Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah”.

notSaid: No word Iddo spoke is recorded; Chronicles names only his writings.
Scripture gives no father or home for him.
He is a different man from the Iddo named as the prophet Zechariah's grandfather after the exile (Zechariah 1:1; Ezra 5:1).

prophets.name: Ahijah
prophets.title: Ahijah the Shilonite, the prophet of Shiloh
prophets.tagline: Tore a new garment into twelve pieces, and later sent Jeroboam's wife home with heavy tidings.

claim.text: Ahijah said the LORD would tear the kingdom from Solomon's son, “because that they have forsaken me”, leaving one tribe for David's sake; Solomon would keep it all his days. Then “Solomon sought therefore to kill Jeroboam”.

Ahijah met Jeroboam alone in the field and gave him ten pieces of a torn garment: ten tribes would be his, and a sure house if he kept the LORD's ways. Years later Jeroboam sent his wife in disguise to ask about their sick son, and Ahijah told her the house of Jeroboam would be cut off.

quote.text: Take thee ten pieces: for thus saith the LORD, the God of Israel, Behold, I will rend the kingdom out of the hand of Solomon, and will give ten tribes to thee:

claim.text: Rehoboam would not listen to the people, “for the cause was from the LORD, that he might perform his saying, which the LORD spake by Ahijah the Shilonite”. Chronicles says the same.

how.text: He acted the word out: he took hold of the new garment, tore it in twelve pieces and told Jeroboam to take ten.
When Jeroboam's wife came disguised, “the LORD said unto Ahijah, Behold, the wife of Jeroboam cometh”, though Ahijah “could not see; for his eyes were set by reason of his age”.
Chronicles names “the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite” as a record of Solomon's acts.

claim.text: Ten tribes would be taken from Solomon's son because they had forsaken the LORD and worshipped Ashtoreth, Chemosh and Milcom; one tribe would stay for David's sake and Jerusalem's.

quotes.text: that David my servant may have a light alway before me in Jerusalem

message.theme: A sure house, on a condition

claim.text: If Jeroboam would walk in the LORD's ways as David did, the LORD would build him “a sure house, as I built for David”.
Because Jeroboam had made other gods and molten images, his house would be swept away and his dead left to dogs and birds.

quotes.text: will take away the remnant of the house of Jeroboam, as a man taketh away dung, till it be all gone.

claim.text: The LORD would root Israel up out of the good land and scatter them beyond the river, because of the sins of Jeroboam.

quotes.text: he shall root up Israel out of this good land, which he gave to their fathers, and shall scatter them beyond the river

claim.text: The child would die when his mother's feet entered the city, and he alone of Jeroboam's house would come to the grave, “because in him there is found some good thing toward the LORD God of Israel”.

quote.text: Take thee ten pieces

words.to: Jeroboam's wife, at his door in Shiloh

quote.text: Come in, thou wife of Jeroboam; why feignest thou thyself to be another? for I am sent to thee with heavy tidings.

claim.text: Ahijah tore a new garment into twelve pieces and gave Jeroboam ten, as a sign of the ten tribes.
Blind with age, he knew Jeroboam's wife at the sound of her feet because the LORD had told him she was coming.

word.text: Ten tribes would be torn from Solomon's son and given to Jeroboam.

reported.text: Kings: Rehoboam would not listen, “that he might perform his saying, which the LORD spake by Ahijah”. Chronicles: “that the LORD might perform his word, which he spake by the hand of Ahijah”.

word.text: The child would die, and all Israel would mourn for him and bury him.

reported.text: When she came to the threshold the child died; “and they buried him; and all Israel mourned for him, according to the word of the LORD, which he spake by the hand of his servant Ahijah the prophet”.

word.text: The house of Jeroboam would be cut off.

reported.text: Baasha smote all the house of Jeroboam “according unto the saying of the LORD, which he spake by his servant Ahijah the Shilonite”.

claim.text: Sent in disguise to ask about her son; Kings does not give her name.
The sick child, in whom “some good thing” was found.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Ahijah met Jeroboam in the way as he went out of Jerusalem

places.name: Shiloh
places.note: Ahijah's home

places.name: Tirzah
places.note: Where the child died as his mother came home

scripture.text: Kings last shows Ahijah old and unable to see; it does not tell of his death.

tradition.text: Rabbinic tradition identified him with Ahiah son of Ahitub, the priest at Shiloh in Saul's time (1 Samuel 14:3), and counted him among seven long-lived saints whose lives span the history of mankind; on this reckoning “Ahijah lived over six hundred years”.
tradition.who: The Midrash and the Talmud (Baba Batra 121b), as reported in the Jewish Encyclopedia

questions.question: Whose new garment did Ahijah tear?

views.label: Ahijah's own
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1872); John Gill (1748–1763); the Pulpit Commentary (1880–1897)

argument.text: Keil: “he rent the new garment, that is to say, his own, not Jeroboam's”; Gill: “not Jeroboam, but the prophet”.

views.label: Jeroboam's
views.holders: H. Ewald, as reported by Keil and the Pulpit Commentary

argument.text: Ewald took “he had clad himself” to mean Jeroboam, and saw in the new garment his “splendid robe of office”.

questions.question: What was the written record Chronicles names for Solomon (“the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite”)?

views.label: Writings used by the Chronicler, perhaps parts of a larger history
views.holders: E. G. Hirsch and W. H. Bennett, Jewish Encyclopedia (1903)

argument.text: They list the prophets' “words”, “visions” and “prophecy” among the Chronicler's sources, and take most of them to be sections of “The Book of the Kings of Israel and Judah”, “probably because the Prophets were supposed to have been the annalists”; for David and Solomon they allow that the references may be to “that portion of the former work which dealt with these kings”. 2 Chronicles 20:34 says the book of Jehu “is mentioned in the book of the kings of Israel”.

views.label: Histories written by the prophets themselves, now lost
views.holders: Matthew Poole (1683–1685); John Gill (1748–1763)

argument.text: Poole takes Iddo's book “concerning genealogies” as “an historical account written by him”; Gill says Iddo “might write the history of his own times”. None of these writings is among the books of the Bible.

notSaid: Scripture gives no father for Ahijah and does not tell how he became a prophet.
Kings does not give the name of Jeroboam's wife.
“The prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite” (2 Chronicles 9:29) is not among the books of the Bible.

prophets.name: Shemaiah
prophets.title: Shemaiah, “the man of God”, in the days of Rehoboam
prophets.tagline: He stopped a war between brothers, and told Rehoboam's princes why Shishak had come.

claim.text: When Rehoboam gathered 180,000 men of Judah and Benjamin to win back the kingdom, the word of God came to Shemaiah, and the army went home. Chronicles adds that when Shishak of Egypt came against Jerusalem, Shemaiah told Rehoboam and the princes that the LORD had left them in Shishak's hand; they humbled themselves, and the LORD granted “some deliverance”.

quote.text: Thus saith the LORD, Ye have forsaken me, and therefore have I also left you in the hand of Shishak.

how.text: “The word of God came unto Shemaiah the man of God, saying, Speak unto Rehoboam”; Chronicles has “the word of the LORD”.
After the princes humbled themselves, “the word of the LORD came to Shemaiah” a second time.
Chronicles names “the book of Shemaiah the prophet” for the acts of Rehoboam.

claim.text: Judah and Benjamin were not to go up against the children of Israel, “for this thing is from me”; they hearkened and went home.

quotes.text: Ye shall not go up, nor fight against your brethren the children of Israel: return every man to his house; for this thing is from me.

claim.text: Rehoboam and all Israel had forsaken the law of the LORD; Shishak took the fenced cities of Judah and came to Jerusalem.

When the princes and the king said “The LORD is righteous”, the word came that they would not be destroyed, but they would serve Shishak, “that they may know my service, and the service of the kingdoms of the countries”.

quotes.text: They have humbled themselves; therefore I will not destroy them, but I will grant them some deliverance

words.to: Rehoboam and the house of Judah and Benjamin

quote.text: Ye shall not go up, nor fight against your brethren the children of Israel

words.to: Rehoboam and the princes of Judah, at Jerusalem

quote.text: Ye have forsaken me, and therefore have I also left you in the hand of Shishak.

claim.text: Their records of Rehoboam's reign are named together.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Where Rehoboam gathered his army, and where the princes gathered because of Shishak

scripture.text: Scripture does not tell of Shemaiah's death.

questions.question: Why does only Chronicles tell Shemaiah's word about Shishak?

views.label: Kings and Chronicles tell it side by side
views.holders: The texts

argument.text: Kings tells Shishak's attack and the treasures he took without naming Shemaiah; Chronicles adds the prophet's word and the princes' humbling. Both books tell the stopped war in nearly the same words.

views.label: Chronicles drew on a prophetic record
views.holders: E. G. Hirsch and W. H. Bennett, Jewish Encyclopedia (1903)

argument.text: Chronicles itself names “the book of Shemaiah the prophet” for Rehoboam's acts; the Jewish Encyclopedia lists “The Words of Shemaiah the Prophet and of Iddo the Seer” among the Chronicler's sources.

notSaid: Scripture gives no father or home for this Shemaiah.
Kings does not mention Shemaiah in its account of Shishak (1 Kings 14:25–28).
Kings says there was war between Rehoboam and Jeroboam “all their days” (1 Kings 14:30) and does not explain how that fits the war Shemaiah stopped.
He is a different man from Shemaiah the Nehelamite (Jeremiah 29:24) and the Shemaiah of Nehemiah 6:10.

prophets.name: Azariah
prophets.title: Azariah son of Oded, on whom “the Spirit of God came”
prophets.tagline: One speech to King Asa, and a reform that followed it.

claim.text: Azariah went out to meet Asa and all Judah and Benjamin. When Asa heard the words he took courage, put away the idols, renewed the altar, and gathered the people to a covenant to seek the LORD.

quote.text: The LORD is with you, while ye be with him; and if ye seek him, he will be found of you; but if ye forsake him, he will forsake you.

how.text: “The Spirit of God came upon Azariah the son of Oded: and he went out to meet Asa”.

message.theme: Seek him and he will be found

claim.text: The LORD would be with them while they were with him; if they forsook him, he would forsake them.

quotes.text: if ye seek him, he will be found of you

message.theme: A people without the true God

claim.text: For a long season Israel was without the true God, a teaching priest and law; but when they turned to the LORD in their trouble he was found of them. In those times there was no peace, “for God did vex them with all adversity”.

quotes.text: Now for a long season Israel hath been without the true God, and without a teaching priest, and without law.

claim.text: He ended with a charge to take courage.

quotes.text: Be ye strong therefore, and let not your hands be weak: for your work shall be rewarded.

words.to: Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin

quote.text: Hear ye me, Asa, and all Judah and Benjamin; The LORD is with you, while ye be with him

claim.text: He is “Azariah the son of Oded”.

scripture.text: Scripture names Azariah only in this chapter and does not tell of his death.

questions.question: What time does Azariah describe in 2 Chronicles 15:3–6?

views.label: The days of the judges
views.holders: Matthew Poole (1683–1685); John Gill (1748–1763); Joseph Benson (1811–1818); C. Vitringa, as reported by Keil

argument.text: Poole: “Generally of the whole nation of Israel in former times, and especially in the times of the judges”; Gill agrees that it refers to “time past”.

views.label: Judah's own recent years
views.holders: Geneva notes (1599); the Syriac and Arabic versions and Rashi, as reported by Keil

argument.text: The Geneva note: “For the space of twelve years under Rehoboam, and three years under Abijah, religion was neglected”.

views.label: The northern kingdom at that time
views.holders: The Targum, Tremellius and Grotius, as reported by Keil

argument.text: Keil reports this view and calls it “decidedly erroneous”, since no such disorder is told of the northern kingdom's first thirty years.

views.label: The future
views.holders: Luther, Clericus and Kimchi, as reported by Keil; William Whiston (1737)

argument.text: Whiston writes that the Hebrew text applies the words “to times past, and not to times future”, which he calls “a very great error”.

views.label: No fixed time: truths for every age
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1872)

argument.text: The verse “contains no verb”; the prophet was “giving utterance to truths which have force at all times”, known in the days of the judges and to be known more deeply later.

views.label: The Chronicler's own reflection
views.holders: W. E. Barnes (1899)

argument.text: Verses 3–6 “contain the reflections of the Chronicler himself on the whole previous course of Israelite history”; Azariah's exhortation continues in verse 7.

notSaid: Kings does not mention Azariah; his speech is in Chronicles only.
Chronicles does not say where Azariah met Asa, only that he “went out to meet Asa” as the king returned from the war with Zerah.
Verse 8 speaks of “the prophecy of Oded the prophet”; who is meant is a question on Oded's page.

prophets.name: Oded
prophets.title: Oded, father of Azariah: “the prophecy of Oded the prophet” (2 Chronicles 15:8)
prophets.tagline: Known from two verses; whether he himself prophesied is a question of the text.

claim.text: “When Asa heard these words, and the prophecy of Oded the prophet, he took courage, and put away the abominable idols”.

how.text: Chronicles names him twice: as the father of Azariah, on whom the Spirit of God came, and in the words “the prophecy of Oded the prophet”.

claim.text: The prophet whose speech to Asa fills 2 Chronicles 15:2–7.

scripture.text: Scripture tells nothing more of Oded.

questions.question: Whose prophecy is “the prophecy of Oded the prophet” in 2 Chronicles 15:8?

views.label: Azariah's, and some words have dropped out
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1872); W. E. Barnes (1899); Ellicott's commentary (c. 1878–1884)

argument.text: W. E. Barnes: “Some words have fallen out of the text. Read, Even the prophecy which Azariah the son of Oded prophesied.” Keil sees no solution but a gloss or a gap; Ellicott suggests “Oded the prophet” may be a marginal gloss and notes there is “no variation in Heb. MSS.” The Latin Vulgate reads “the prophecy of Azarias the son of Oded the prophet” (Douay-Rheims); the Greek reads “the prophecy of Adad the prophet” (Brenton).

views.label: Azariah's, called by his father's name
views.holders: Matthew Poole (1683–1685); Joseph Benson (1811–1818); John Gill (1748–1763)

argument.text: Poole: “Of Azariah … who was also called by his father’s name Oded”, or “the son of” is understood; Gill: “rather Oded here is the same with the son of Oded”.

views.label: A prophecy of Oded the father, not recorded
views.holders: “Some”, as reported by Poole and Gill; the Pulpit Commentary allows it

argument.text: Azariah may have repeated an older prophecy of his father. The Pulpit Commentary says this is “open to possibility” but “not very likely”.

views.label: Oded is Iddo
views.holders: Jerome, as reported by the Jewish Encyclopedia (1904)

argument.text: Jerome “identifies Iddo also with the Oded of II Chron. xv. 8”; Keil calls this conjecture without “tenable foundation”.

notSaid: No words of Oded are recorded.
Chronicles does not say whether Oded was alive in Asa's day.
He is a different man from the Oded who met Israel's army at Samaria in the days of Ahaz (2 Chronicles 28:9).

prophets.name: Hanani
prophets.title: Hanani the seer, imprisoned by King Asa
prophets.tagline: He told Asa he had relied on the king of Syria, and was put in prison for it.

claim.text: After Asa paid Ben-hadad of Syria to break his league with Baasha, Hanani the seer came to him with a rebuke. “Asa was wroth with the seer, and put him in a prison house”.

quote.text: Herein thou hast done foolishly: therefore from henceforth thou shalt have wars.

how.text: Chronicles calls him “Hanani the seer”; he “came to Asa king of Judah” and told him what his reliance on the king of Syria had cost. The text does not say how the word came to him.

claim.text: Because Asa had relied on the king of Syria and not on the LORD, the host of Syria had escaped his hand; when he had relied on the LORD against the Ethiopians and Lubims, the LORD delivered them to him.

quotes.text: Because thou hast relied on the king of Syria, and not relied on the LORD thy God, therefore is the host of the king of Syria escaped out of thine hand.

claim.text: The LORD looks over the whole earth to show himself strong for those whose heart is perfect toward him.

quotes.text: For the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to shew himself strong in the behalf of them whose heart is perfect toward him.

quote.text: Herein thou hast done foolishly: therefore from henceforth thou shalt have wars.

claim.text: The king Asa paid with the treasures of the house of the LORD; Hanani's rebuke is about relying on him.
Kings and Chronicles name a prophet “Jehu the son of Hanani”; whether his father is this seer is a question below.

scripture.text: Asa put him “in a prison house”; Scripture does not say whether or when he was set free.

questions.question: Is Hanani the seer the father of the prophet Jehu?

views.label: Yes
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1872); the Pulpit Commentary (1880–1897); Ellicott's commentary and the Jewish Encyclopedia, more cautiously

argument.text: Keil: Jehu “was without doubt his son”; the Pulpit Commentary says “Presumably”, Ellicott “perhaps”, and the Jewish Encyclopedia “probably”. The site's person data treats them as father and son.

views.label: Scripture does not say
views.holders: W. E. Barnes (1899)

argument.text: Barnes notes only that “Hanani as a seer is known to us from this passage only”, while Jehu is elsewhere called “son of Hanani”.

notSaid: Kings does not mention Hanani's rebuke or his imprisonment; they are in Chronicles only.
Chronicles goes on to tell Asa's disease in his feet (2 Chronicles 16:12) but does not link it to Hanani's word.
Scripture does not say what became of Hanani after the prison house.

prophets.name: Jehu
prophets.title: Jehu son of Hanani, prophet to Baasha and to Jehoshaphat
prophets.tagline: He told Baasha his house would fall like Jeroboam's, and asked Jehoshaphat, “Shouldest thou help the ungodly?”

claim.text: The word of the LORD came to Jehu against Baasha: raised “out of the dust”, Baasha had walked in Jeroboam's way, and his house would be made like Jeroboam's.

quote.text: Behold, I will take away the posterity of Baasha, and the posterity of his house; and will make thy house like the house of Jeroboam the son of Nebat.

claim.text: Zimri killed Baasha's son Elah and all his house, “according to the word of the LORD, which he spake against Baasha by Jehu the prophet”.
When Jehoshaphat came home from fighting beside Ahab, Jehu went out to meet him with rebuke and praise. Chronicles says the acts of Jehoshaphat are written “in the book of Jehu the son of Hanani”.

quote.text: Shouldest thou help the ungodly, and love them that hate the LORD? therefore is wrath upon thee from before the LORD.

how.text: “Then the word of the LORD came to Jehu the son of Hanani against Baasha”; Kings says it came again “by the hand of the prophet Jehu”.
Chronicles names “the book of Jehu the son of Hanani, who is mentioned in the book of the kings of Israel”.

The same name and father are given under Baasha and under Jehoshaphat, more than thirty years apart; commentators take him to be one man (the Jewish Encyclopedia: he “must have either lived to a very great age or begun his prophetical career very young”).

claim.text: The LORD had exalted Baasha “out of the dust”, and Baasha had made Israel sin; his house would be swept away.

quotes.text: Forasmuch as I exalted thee out of the dust, and made thee prince over my people Israel

claim.text: Jehoshaphat had helped “the ungodly”, and wrath was on him; yet good things were found in him.

quotes.text: Nevertheless there are good things found in thee, in that thou hast taken away the groves out of the land, and hast prepared thine heart to seek God.

quote.text: Forasmuch as I exalted thee out of the dust, and made thee prince over my people Israel
Shouldest thou help the ungodly, and love them that hate the LORD?

word.text: Baasha's posterity would be taken away and his house made like Jeroboam's.

reported.text: Zimri slew all the house of Baasha, “according to the word of the LORD, which he spake against Baasha by Jehu the prophet”.

claim.text: He is “Jehu the son of Hanani”; whether this is Hanani the seer is a question on Hanani's page.

scripture.text: He was alive to meet Jehoshaphat, and Chronicles names his book as the record of Jehoshaphat's acts; it does not tell of his death.

tradition.text: The Latin Vulgate reads 1 Kings 16:7 as Baasha killing Jehu: “for this cause he slew him, that is to say, Jehu the son of Hanani, the prophet” (Douay-Rheims). Chronicles, which has Jehu meet Jehoshaphat later, does not fit this reading.
tradition.who: The Latin Vulgate (Jerome's translation), as printed in the Clementine edition

questions.question: Who is “him” in “because he killed him” (1 Kings 16:7)?

views.label: Nadab, Jeroboam's son
views.holders: Matthew Poole (1683–1685); Joseph Benson (1811–1818); the Pulpit Commentary (1880–1897)

argument.text: Poole: “i.e. Nadab; who, though he be not expressed, yet is sufficiently understood”; Baasha killed Nadab (1 Kings 15:27–28).

views.label: Jeroboam's whole house
views.holders: Abarbanel, as reported by John Gill

argument.text: Gill reports that it “may refer, as Abarbinel thinks, to the whole house of Jeroboam”; he himself prefers Nadab.

views.label: Jehu the prophet
views.holders: The Latin Vulgate

argument.text: The Vulgate adds words that the Douay-Rheims renders “that is to say, Jehu the son of Hanani, the prophet”; the Jewish Encyclopedia calls this a gloss.

notSaid: Scripture does not say where Jehu lived, or how he came from prophesying against Israel's king to meeting Judah's.
It does not tell of his death; the Vulgate's reading of 1 Kings 16:7 is shown under Tradition.
This Jehu is a different man from Jehu son of Nimshi, who became king of Israel (2 Kings 9:2).

prophets.name: Jahaziel
prophets.title: Jahaziel the Levite, “of the sons of Asaph”
prophets.tagline: In the assembly before Jehoshaphat: “the battle is not yours, but God’s.”

claim.text: When Moab, Ammon and others came against Judah, Jehoshaphat proclaimed a fast and prayed in the house of the LORD. The Spirit of the LORD came on Jahaziel “in the midst of the congregation”, and he told them where the enemy would come and that they would not need to fight. Chronicles goes on: as the singers praised, the LORD set ambushments, and the attackers destroyed one another.

quote.text: Be not afraid nor dismayed by reason of this great multitude; for the battle is not yours, but God’s.

how.text: “Then upon Jahaziel … came the Spirit of the LORD in the midst of the congregation”; he spoke with “Thus saith the LORD unto you”.

claim.text: Judah was not to fear the great multitude.

quotes.text: for the battle is not yours, but God’s.

claim.text: They were to go down the next day by the cliff of Ziz to the end of the brook before the wilderness of Jeruel, but they would not need to fight.

quotes.text: set yourselves, stand ye still, and see the salvation of the LORD with you, O Judah and Jerusalem

words.to: all Judah, Jerusalem and King Jehoshaphat

quote.text: Hearken ye, all Judah, and ye inhabitants of Jerusalem, and thou king Jehoshaphat

claim.text: Jahaziel was “a Levite of the sons of Asaph”.
His line is given back four generations: “the son of Zechariah, the son of Benaiah, the son of Jeiel, the son of Mattaniah”.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: The assembly in the house of the LORD where the Spirit came on him

places.name: Cliff of Ziz
places.note: Where he said the enemy would come up

places.name: Wilderness of Tekoa
places.note: Where Judah went out the next morning

places.name: Valley of Berachah
places.note: Where they blessed the LORD on the fourth day

scripture.text: Scripture names Jahaziel only here.

notSaid: Kings does not tell this war or Jahaziel's word; it is in Chronicles only.
Chronicles does not use the words “according to the word of the LORD” of the victory; it tells what happened next.
Nothing else is told of Jahaziel.

prophets.name: Eliezer
prophets.title: Eliezer son of Dodavah, of Mareshah
prophets.tagline: One sentence against Jehoshaphat's ships, in Chronicles only.

claim.text: Jehoshaphat joined Ahaziah of Israel to make ships at Ezion-geber to go to Tarshish; Eliezer prophesied against him, “And the ships were broken, that they were not able to go to Tarshish.”

quote.text: Because thou hast joined thyself with Ahaziah, the LORD hath broken thy works.

claim.text: The partner in the venture; Chronicles says he “did very wickedly”.

how.text: “Then Eliezer the son of Dodavah of Mareshah prophesied against Jehoshaphat, saying”.

claim.text: Because Jehoshaphat had joined himself with Ahaziah, the LORD had broken his works.

quotes.text: the LORD hath broken thy works

quote.text: Because thou hast joined thyself with Ahaziah, the LORD hath broken thy works.

claim.text: He is “Eliezer the son of Dodavah of Mareshah”.

places.name: Mareshah
places.note: His home

places.name: Ezion-geber
places.note: Where the ships were made and broken

scripture.text: Scripture names Eliezer only here.

questions.question: How do Kings and Chronicles tell the broken ships?

views.label: Side by side
views.holders: The texts

argument.text: Kings: Jehoshaphat made ships “to go to Ophir for gold”, they were broken at Ezion-geber, and when Ahaziah asked to send his servants in the ships, “Jehoshaphat would not”. Chronicles: Jehoshaphat joined Ahaziah to make ships “to go to Tarshish”, Eliezer prophesied, and the ships were broken. Kings does not name Eliezer.

views.label: One sequence: the joint fleet was wrecked, then Jehoshaphat refused a second venture
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1872); Matthew Poole (1683–1685); the Pulpit Commentary (1880–1897)

argument.text: Keil: Ahaziah wanted another attempt after the first ships were broken, and Jehoshaphat refused “after the fulfilment of Eliezer's prediction”. He takes Chronicles' “to go to Tarshish” to have sprung “from an erroneous interpretation of the expression ‘ships of Tarshish’”.

views.label: The common source is out of order
views.holders: The Pulpit Commentary on Chronicles (1880–1897)

argument.text: The “dislocation of both manner and matter” in both accounts “probably betrays something out of order … in the more original source, from which both drew”.

notSaid: Kings does not mention Eliezer or a partnership in the broken ships.
Nothing else is told of Eliezer.

prophets.name: Zechariah
prophets.title: Zechariah son of Jehoiada the priest, stoned in the court of the house of the LORD
prophets.tagline: “The LORD look upon it, and require it.”

claim.text: After Jehoiada died, the princes of Judah came to the king and he hearkened to them; they left the house of the LORD and served groves and idols. The Spirit of God came upon Zechariah, and he warned the people; they conspired against him and stoned him “at the commandment of the king in the court of the house of the LORD”. Joash “remembered not the kindness which Jehoiada his father had done to him, but slew his son”.

quote.text: Why transgress ye the commandments of the LORD, that ye cannot prosper? because ye have forsaken the LORD, he hath also forsaken you.

how.text: “The Spirit of God came upon Zechariah the son of Jehoiada the priest, which stood above the people”; he spoke with “Thus saith God”.
Just before, Chronicles says of the time after Jehoiada's death: “Yet he sent prophets to them, to bring them again unto the LORD”.

claim.text: They could not prosper while they broke the commandments; because they had forsaken the LORD, he had forsaken them.

quotes.text: because ye have forsaken the LORD, he hath also forsaken you.

quote.text: Why transgress ye the commandments of the LORD, that ye cannot prosper?

claim.text: Jehoiada had saved Joash and made him king; he died aged a hundred and thirty and was buried among the kings.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: The court of the house of the LORD

scripture.text: He was stoned in the court of the house of the LORD at the king's command, and as he died he said, “The LORD look upon it, and require it.”

Chronicles goes on: at the end of the year the Syrians came and “executed judgment against Joash”, and his own servants slew him on his bed “for the blood of the sons of Jehoiada the priest”. It does not say here that this came according to Zechariah's word.

Jesus spoke of “the blood of Zacharias son of Barachias, whom ye slew between the temple and the altar” (Matthew); Luke has “the blood of Zacharias, which perished between the altar and the temple”. Whether this is the same man is a question below.

tradition.text: The Rabbis said Zechariah was killed in the priests' court on a Sabbath that was also the Day of Atonement, and that when Nebuzar-adan came to destroy the Temple his blood “began to boil”; Nebuzar-adan killed many thousands to appease it, until he cried out to Zechariah and the blood was still.
tradition.who: The Talmud (Gittin 57b; Sanhedrin 96b) and Lamentations Rabbah, as reported by the Jewish Encyclopedia

questions.question: Is he the “Zacharias son of Barachias” of Matthew 23:35?

views.label: Yes; Jehoiada had a second name, or was the grandfather
views.holders: Geneva notes (1599); Albert Barnes (1832); the Pulpit Commentary on Matthew (1880–1897), as possibilities

argument.text: The Geneva note: “Of Joiada, who was also called Barach-jah”. Barnes notes that it was common to have two names. The Pulpit Commentary also allows that Barachiah was the father and Jehoiada the grandfather. Ellicott calls such suggestions “hypotheses invented for the occasion, without a shadow of evidence”.

views.label: Yes; “son of Barachias” is a slip or a later addition
views.holders: Ellicott's commentary (c. 1878–1884); A. Carr (1878); H. A. W. Meyer (1879)

argument.text: Luke 11:51 has no father's name, and Jerome reports that the Gospel of the Nazarenes read “son of Joiada” (Pulpit Commentary). Ellicott: “the mistake of a transcriber”; Carr: the words “are possibly interpolated”; Meyer: an error from confusing him with the prophet Zechariah son of Berechiah (Zechariah 1:1). Carr and Meyer add that from Abel to this Zechariah runs from Genesis to Chronicles, the first and last books of the Hebrew canon.

views.label: No; the prophet Zechariah son of Berechiah
views.holders: William Whiston (1737); “others”, as reported by Albert Barnes (1832)

argument.text: Whiston: “Zechariah the prophet was really ‘the son of Barachiah’”, and of how he died “we have no other account than that before us in St. Matthew”.

views.label: No; another Zacharias
views.holders: “Some commentators”, reported by A. Carr (1878), the Pulpit Commentary and Whiston (Zacharias son of Baruch); a tradition reported by Origen, as the Pulpit Commentary notes (John the Baptist's father)

argument.text: Some took the words as foretelling the Zacharias son of Baruch whom zealots killed “in the middle of the temple” during the Jewish war (Josephus, War 4.5.4); Carr calls this “hardly probable”, and Whiston “a somewhat strange exposition”. Origen reported a tradition that it was John the Baptist's father, which the Pulpit Commentary says “looks as if it was made to relieve the difficulty”.

notSaid: Chronicles does not call Zechariah a prophet in so many words; it says the Spirit of God came upon him, after saying the LORD “sent prophets to them”.
Chronicles places his death “in the court of the house of the LORD”; it does not say “between the temple and the altar”.
Kings does not tell Zechariah's death; it is in Chronicles only.

prophets.name: Zechariah
prophets.title: Zechariah, “who had understanding in the visions of God” (2 Chronicles 26:5)
prophets.tagline: Uzziah sought God in his days; one verse is all Scripture gives.

claim.text: “He sought God in the days of Zechariah, who had understanding in the visions of God: and as long as he sought the LORD, God made him to prosper.”

how.text: Chronicles says he “had understanding in the visions of God”; another reading is a question below.

scripture.text: Scripture tells nothing more of him.

questions.question: “In the visions of God” or “in the fear of God”?

views.label: “Visions”, as the Hebrew written text reads
views.holders: The King James Version; the Latin Vulgate (“that understood and saw God”, Douay-Rheims)

argument.text: The Pulpit Commentary notes that “either reading” leaves a good meaning.

views.label: “Fear”, by a small change of letters
views.holders: The Greek Septuagint (Brenton: “who understood the fear of the Lord”); C. F. Keil (1872); W. E. Barnes (1899); Ellicott's commentary

argument.text: Ellicott says some Hebrew manuscripts, the Septuagint, Syriac, Arabic and Targum read “in the fear of God”, and calls it “doubtless correct”; Keil renders “who instructed him in the fear of God”; Barnes: “Read, in the fear of God”.

questions.question: Who was this Zechariah?

views.label: Otherwise unknown
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1872); W. E. Barnes (1899); Ellicott's commentary; the Pulpit Commentary

argument.text: Keil: “Nothing further is known of the Zechariah here mentioned”; Barnes: “Nothing is known (apart from this passage)”.

views.label: Perhaps a son of Zechariah son of Jehoiada, or the Zechariah of Isaiah 8:2
views.holders: Joseph Benson (1811–1818); John Gill (1748–1763)

argument.text: Benson: “probably the son of that Zechariah whom his grand-father Joash slew”; Gill: “as it may seem, a son of his, perhaps the same with him in Isaiah 8:2”. The Geneva note says only that he “was not the Zechariah that was the son of Jehoiada”.

notSaid: Chronicles does not call this Zechariah a prophet or a priest.
It does not say when he died, or link his death to Uzziah's pride in 2 Chronicles 26:16.
Kings does not mention him.

prophets.name: Oded
prophets.title: Oded, “a prophet of the LORD” in Samaria
prophets.tagline: He met Israel's army at Samaria and told them to send their captives home.

claim.text: Pekah son of Remaliah slew a hundred and twenty thousand in Judah in one day, and Israel carried away two hundred thousand captives to Samaria. Oded went out before the host that came to Samaria.

quote.text: Now hear me therefore, and deliver the captives again, which ye have taken captive of your brethren: for the fierce wrath of the LORD is upon you.

claim.text: The captives were Ahaz's people of Judah and Jerusalem, delivered into Israel's hand because of the wrath of the LORD.

how.text: “But a prophet of the LORD was there, whose name was Oded: and he went out before the host”.

message.theme: A rage that reaches to heaven

claim.text: The LORD had delivered Judah into their hand in his wrath, but they had slain them in a rage beyond measure.

quotes.text: ye have slain them in a rage that reacheth up unto heaven.

claim.text: They meant to make their brethren bondmen and bondwomen, but they had sins of their own against the LORD.

quotes.text: but are there not with you, even with you, sins against the LORD your God?

claim.text: They were to return the captives, for the fierce wrath of the LORD was upon them.

quote.text: deliver the captives again, which ye have taken captive of your brethren

person.name: Azariah, Berechiah, Jehizkiah and Amasa, heads of Ephraim

claim.text: They stood up against the returning soldiers and refused to let the captives in; the men named took the captives, clothed, fed and anointed them, and brought them to Jericho.

places.name: Samaria
places.note: Where Oded met the army

places.name: Jericho, the city of palm trees
places.note: Where the captives were brought to their brethren

scripture.text: Scripture names Oded only here.

notSaid: Kings does not tell this episode; it is in Chronicles only.
Chronicles does not say Oded spoke to Pekah himself; he spoke to the army.
He is a different man from Oded the father of Azariah (2 Chronicles 15:1).

prophets.name: Huldah
prophets.title: Huldah the prophetess, in Josiah's Jerusalem
prophets.tagline: Asked about the book found in the temple, she answered for the LORD: evil on “this place”, peace for the king.

claim.text: When the book of the law was found and read to him, Josiah rent his clothes and sent Hilkiah the priest and four others to enquire of the LORD; they went to Huldah. Her answer came back to the king, and he gathered the elders, read the book to the people and made a covenant.

quote.text: Because thine heart was tender, and thou hast humbled thyself before the LORD

how.text: The king's men “went unto Huldah the prophetess … and they communed with her”.
She answered in the LORD's name: “Thus saith the LORD God of Israel, Tell the man that sent you to me”.

claim.text: The LORD would bring evil on “this place” and its people, because they had forsaken him and burned incense to other gods. Kings says “even all the words of the book which the king of Judah hath read”; Chronicles says “all the curses that are written in the book”.

quotes.text: therefore my wrath shall be kindled against this place, and shall not be quenched.

claim.text: Because Josiah humbled himself, rent his clothes and wept, he would be gathered to his grave in peace and not see the evil.

quotes.text: thou shalt be gathered into thy grave in peace; and thine eyes shall not see all the evil which I will bring upon this place.

quote.text: Tell the man that sent you to me
Because thine heart was tender, and thou hast humbled thyself before the LORD

claim.text: “The wife of Shallum the son of Tikvah, the son of Harhas, keeper of the wardrobe”; Chronicles spells the names Tikvath and Hasrah.
He found the book, and is named first among the men sent to her.
One of the five sent to her.
He read the book before the king and went with the others.
One of the five in Kings; Chronicles names “Abdon the son of Micah” in his place.

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: She “dwelt in Jerusalem in the college”; what that means is a question below

scripture.text: Scripture tells nothing more of Huldah after her answer to the king.

questions.question: What was “the college” where she lived?

views.label: A school or house of instruction
views.holders: The Targum, as reported by Ellicott and Gill; Geneva notes (1599); Matthew Poole (1683–1685)

argument.text: The Geneva note: “Or the house of doctrine, which was near the temple”. Poole: “where the sons of the prophets, or others who devoted themselves to the study of God's word, used to meet”.

views.label: A district of the city, “the second quarter”
views.holders: Ellicott's commentary; J. R. Lumby (1887); C. F. Keil (1872); the Pulpit Commentary

argument.text: The Hebrew mishneh means “second”, as in “an howling from the second” (Zephaniah 1:10) and “second over the city” (Nehemiah 11:9). Ellicott: “The word really means the second part of the city”; the Revised Version reads “in the second quarter” (Lumby).

questions.question: Why did the king's men go to Huldah?

views.label: Scripture gives no reason
views.holders: The text

argument.text: Kings and Chronicles say only that they went to her and that she dwelt in Jerusalem.

views.label: Jeremiah and Zephaniah were not in Jerusalem at the time
views.holders: Ellicott's commentary; C. F. Keil (1872); the Pulpit Commentary (“Possibly”)

argument.text: Keil: “none of the prophets of renown, such as Jeremiah and Zephaniah, were at that time in Jerusalem”.

views.label: A woman would be more moved to pity
views.holders: The Talmud (Megillah 14a–b), as reported by the Jewish Encyclopedia (1904)

argument.text: The king “thought that women are more easily stirred to pity than men”, so the prophetess “would be more likely than Jeremiah to intercede with God in his behalf”.

questions.question: “Gathered into thy grave in peace” — yet Josiah was killed in battle. How is that read?

views.label: Peace means before the ruin of the city
views.holders: C. F. Keil (1872); J. R. Lumby (1887); the Pulpit Commentary; Ellicott's commentary

argument.text: Keil: “in peace, i.e., without living to witness the devastation of Jerusalem”; Lumby: “The promise has no reference to the war with Egypt”. Kings tells that Pharaoh-nechoh slew him at Megiddo; Chronicles that archers wounded him and he died after being brought to Jerusalem.

views.label: Peace with God
views.holders: Matthew Henry (1706–1721); Matthew Poole (1683–1685); John Gill (1748–1763)

argument.text: Henry: “Though Josiah was mortally wounded in battle, yet he died in peace with God”; Poole and Gill give this beside the first view.

notSaid: Scripture names Huldah only in this one event, told in Kings and in Chronicles.
It does not say why she, rather than another prophet, was consulted.

Kings and Chronicles do not themselves say that her word came to pass; they tell Josiah's covenant, his death at Megiddo and, later, the fall of Jerusalem. 2 Kings 24:2 sends the bands against Judah “according to the word of the LORD, which he spake by his servants the prophets”, without naming her.

prophets.name: Urijah
prophets.title: Urijah son of Shemaiah of Kirjath-jearim
prophets.tagline: He prophesied as Jeremiah did, fled to Egypt, and was brought back and killed by Jehoiakim.

claim.text: When Jehoiakim, his mighty men and the princes heard Urijah's words, the king sought to kill him. Urijah fled to Egypt; the king sent Elnathan son of Achbor and others, who brought him back.

quote.text: who slew him with the sword, and cast his dead body into the graves of the common people.

how.text: “There was also a man that prophesied in the name of the LORD, Urijah”.

message.theme: Against the city and the land

claim.text: He “prophesied against this city and against this land according to all the words of Jeremiah”. Jeremiah gives none of his own words.
Urijah's words matched Jeremiah's; the chapter ends that Ahikam's hand was with Jeremiah, so that he was not put to death.
Sent by Jehoiakim to bring him back from Egypt.
He was “the son of Shemaiah of Kirjath-jearim”.

places.name: Kirjath-jearim
places.note: His home

places.name: Egypt
places.note: Where he fled and was taken

places.name: Jerusalem
places.note: Where Jehoiakim reigned; Jeremiah 26:23 says only that Urijah was brought “unto Jehoiakim the king” and killed

scripture.text: Brought back from Egypt to Jehoiakim, “who slew him with the sword, and cast his dead body into the graves of the common people”.

questions.question: Who tells Urijah's story in Jeremiah 26?

views.label: The writer, to show Jeremiah's danger
views.holders: Ellicott's commentary; C. F. Keil (1874–1880); the Pulpit Commentary; A. W. Streane (1913)

argument.text: It is not part of the elders' speech: Ellicott says it “cannot be regarded as part of the argument of the ‘elders’”; Streane: “The story is introduced by the compiler (probably Baruch) to illustrate the risk to which Jeremiah was exposed”; Keil: to show “the hostility of King Jehoiakim”.

views.label: The elders, as a warning
views.holders: R. Jamieson, A. R. Fausset and D. Brown (1871); one opinion reported by Joseph Benson

argument.text: JFB: the context “implies rather that the words are the continuation of the previous speech of the elders”: Urijah suffered, and they imply that “sin has been added”.

views.label: Jeremiah's accusers, as a precedent for death
views.holders: Matthew Poole (1683–1685); John Gill (1748–1763), after Kimchi and Rashi

argument.text: Poole: “the words of some others … urging a later precedent, in the time of Jehoiakim”; Gill reports Kimchi and Jarchi (Rashi) reading it so.

notSaid: Jeremiah does not record any of Urijah's words, only that they agreed with Jeremiah's.
It does not give the year of his death; the chapter's opening date (“the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim”, Jeremiah 26:1) belongs to Jeremiah's own trial.
Scripture does not say he was beheaded; it says Jehoiakim “slew him with the sword”.
